polymer-chem-001.question: Which polymer is made by condensation polymerization?
choices: Polyethylene, made from ethylene, CH2=CH2
Polystyrene, made from styrene, CH2=CHC6H5
Nylon 66, made from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid
polymer-chem-001.explanation: Condensation polymerization is polymerization in which a small molecule such as water is released each time two functional groups react to form a bond. In nylon 66, an amino group, −NH2, and a carboxy group, −COOH, react to form an amide bond, −CONH−, releasing one molecule of H2O each time. Ethylene and styrene undergo addition polymerization, linking by opening their C=C double bonds; all the atoms of the monomer end up in the polymer, and no by-product is released. As a result, the repeat unit of an addition polymer has the same composition as the monomer, while the repeat unit of a condensation polymer has the composition of the monomers combined minus the molecules released.

polymer-chem-002.question: For the radical polymerization of styrene, 2,2'-azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN), (CH3)2C(CN)−N=N−C(CN)(CH3)2, was added and the mixture heated to about 60–70 °C. What is the role of AIBN?
choices: It decomposes on heating to release nitrogen, N2, and the carbon radicals formed add to the monomer to initiate polymerization
It acts as a chain-transfer agent that donates hydrogen atoms to growing radicals to stop the chains and control molecular weight
It acts as a polymerization inhibitor that reacts rapidly with growing radicals to stop polymerization
polymer-chem-002.explanation: AIBN is a typical radical initiator. On heating, it cleaves on both sides of the N=N bond, releasing N2 and giving two 2-cyano-2-propyl radicals, (CH3)2C(CN)·. This radical adds to the C=C of styrene to form a new radical; that is the initiation step. Then come propagation, in which monomers add one after another, and termination, in which radicals react with each other and disappear. The release of N2 drives the decomposition, and its rate being little affected by the solvent is why AIBN is convenient to use. Chain-transfer agents for controlling molecular weight are compounds such as thiols, and polymerization inhibitors are compounds such as hydroquinone; both play roles different from AIBN's.

polymer-chem-003.question: Among the termination reactions of radical polymerization, which correctly describes termination by disproportionation?
choices: The ends of two growing radicals bond to each other, giving one polymer chain with the combined length of the two
One growing radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, giving one chain with a saturated end and one with a terminal C=C
A growing radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from the solvent and stops, and the solvent radical starts a new chain
polymer-chem-003.explanation: Termination is the reaction in which two growing radicals meet and their unpaired electrons disappear, and it comes in two kinds, combination and disproportionation. In disproportionation, one radical abstracts a hydrogen atom at the β position of the other chain, giving two polymers, one with a saturated end and one with a C=C double bond at its end. Joining the ends of two chains so that their lengths add up is combination. Styrene is said to terminate mainly by combination and methyl methacrylate mainly by disproportionation. Abstraction of hydrogen from the solvent or a thiol to start a new chain is chain transfer; the number of radicals does not decrease, so it is distinguished from termination.

polymer-chem-004.question: 1.0 g of a polymer with molecular weight 1.0×10⁴ is mixed with 1.0 g of a polymer with molecular weight 3.0×10⁴ (assume each is uniform in molecular weight). What is the number-average molecular weight Mn of the mixture?
polymer-chem-004.explanation: The number-average molecular weight is the total mass divided by the total amount in moles. The amounts are 1.0 g/1.0×10⁴ = 1.0×10⁻⁴ mol and 1.0 g/3.0×10⁴ ≈ 3.33×10⁻⁵ mol, totaling 1.33×10⁻⁴ mol. Mn = 2.0 g/1.33×10⁻⁴ mol = 1.5×10⁴. 2.0×10⁴ is the mass-weighted average, which corresponds to the weight-average molecular weight Mw = (1.0×1.0×10⁴ + 1.0×3.0×10⁴)/2.0. 2.5×10⁴ is Mw when equal amounts in moles are mixed. Mn is pulled toward the numerous small molecules and Mw toward the heavy ones, so whenever there is a distribution Mw > Mn; the dispersity in this example is Mw/Mn ≈ 1.33.

polymer-chem-005.question: In a step-growth polymerization (polycondensation) of a diol and a dicarboxylic acid in equal molar amounts, what is the theoretical dispersity Mw/Mn (from Flory's most probable distribution) as the extent of reaction p approaches 1?
polymer-chem-005.explanation: If the reactivity of a functional group is independent of chain length, the molecular-weight distribution of a step-growth polymerization is Flory's most probable distribution, and from Mn ∝ 1/(1 − p) and Mw ∝ (1 + p)/(1 − p), the dispersity is Mw/Mn = 1 + p. As p → 1, Mw/Mn approaches 2. 1.0 is the ideal case in which all molecules have the same length; living anionic polymerization gives values close to 1. 1.5 is the theoretical value for radical polymerization terminating only by combination; termination by disproportionation gives 2. Dispersity expresses the breadth of the molecular-weight distribution and is never smaller than 1.

polymer-chem-006.question: In the radical (chain-growth) polymerization of styrene, what is the state of the reaction mixture early in the reaction, when monomer conversion is still only a few percent?
choices: Monomers are gradually linking into dimers and trimers, and no high-molecular-weight polymer exists yet
High-molecular-weight polymer has already formed, and most of the rest is unreacted monomer
The monomer is almost all consumed, but mostly as oligomers of still low molecular weight
polymer-chem-006.explanation: In chain-growth polymerization, an initiated radical adds hundreds to thousands of monomers during its short lifetime of a few seconds or less and then terminates, so high-molecular-weight polymer forms from the very beginning of the reaction. At low conversion, the mixture consists of this polymer and unreacted monomer, with very few chains still growing. Gradually linking into dimers and trimers, with the monomer consumed quickly but the molecular weight slow to rise, is characteristic of step-growth polymerization (polycondensation); the other two choices describe the early and middle stages of step-growth polymerization. In short, in chain-growth polymerization it is mainly the yield that increases with time, while in step-growth polymerization it is the molecular weight.

polymer-chem-007.question: A diol and a dicarboxylic acid were polycondensed in equal molar amounts. When the extent of reaction of the functional groups reaches p = 0.99, what is the number-average degree of polymerization Xn from the Carothers equation, Xn = 1/(1 − p)?
polymer-chem-007.explanation: The Carothers equation is derived from the ratio of the number of molecules at the start, N0, to the number at extent of reaction p, N = N0(1 − p), giving Xn = N0/N = 1/(1 − p). At p = 0.99, Xn = 1/0.01 = 100. 99 computes p/(1 − p), and 50 divides by 2, as in 1/(2(1 − p)). As the equation shows, even at an extent of reaction of 0.95, Xn is only 20, and it finally reaches 200 at p = 0.995. Obtaining high molecular weight in condensation polymerization requires an extremely high extent of reaction, so the by-product water is removed under reduced pressure to push the equilibrium toward the products. Xn here is the number of monomer units (counting one diol and one dicarboxylic acid each as 1).

polymer-chem-008.question: In the polycondensation of a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid, the charge had a functional-group ratio r = 0.98 (minority functional group/majority functional group), and the extent of reaction of the minority group reached p = 0.99. Using Xn = (1 + r)/(1 + r − 2rp), which value is closest to the number-average degree of polymerization Xn?
polymer-chem-008.explanation: Substituting into the equation, Xn = (1 + 0.98)/(1 + 0.98 − 2 × 0.98 × 0.99) = 1.98/(1.98 − 1.9404) = 1.98/0.0396 = 50. 100 ignores the imbalance and calculates 1/(1 − p), and 99 is (1 + r)/(1 − r), the value for p = 1 (the limit of complete reaction). An imbalance of only 2% halves the degree of polymerization, from 100 for equal amounts to 50. This is because the majority functional group caps both ends of the chains; for nylon 66, a 1 : 1 salt (nylon salt) is made from the diamine and adipic acid and purified before polymerization to set the ratio exactly to 1. Conversely, a small amount of a monofunctional monomer is sometimes added to hold down the molecular weight deliberately.

polymer-chem-009.question: In a radical polymerization, only the initiator concentration is quadrupled, with the monomer concentration and temperature unchanged. If the steady-state approximation holds, termination occurs by reaction of two radicals, and chain transfer is negligible, how do the polymerization rate and the molecular weight of the polymer change?
choices: The polymerization rate quadruples, and the molecular weight is unchanged
The polymerization rate doubles, and the molecular weight also doubles
The polymerization rate doubles, and the molecular weight falls to about 1/2
polymer-chem-009.explanation: At steady state, the rate of radical formation balances the rate of termination, and the radical concentration is proportional to [I]^(1/2). The polymerization rate Rp = kp[M][R·] is also proportional to [I]^(1/2), so quadrupling [I] increases Rp by √4 = 2. On the other hand, the number of monomers a chain adds before terminating (the kinetic chain length) is propagation rate/termination rate ∝ [M]/[I]^(1/2), so the molecular weight falls to about 1/2. The more radicals there are, the more readily they meet one another and terminate. A fourfold rate overlooks the square-root relationship, and a doubled molecular weight assumes that rate and molecular weight move in the same direction. When both the rate and the molecular weight need to be raised at once, methods such as emulsion polymerization are used.

polymer-chem-010.question: A small amount of 1-dodecanethiol, C12H25SH, was added to the radical polymerization of methyl methacrylate. What is the main effect of this addition?
choices: Growing radicals abstract the S−H hydrogen and stop, and the RS· radicals formed start new chains, lowering the molecular weight with little change in rate
The thiol decomposes like an initiator to make more radicals, so the radical concentration rises and both rate and molecular weight increase greatly
The thiol traps growing radicals to form an unreactive, stable radical, so polymerization stops completely
polymer-chem-010.explanation: Thiols are typical chain-transfer agents. When a growing radical P· abstracts the hydrogen of the weak S−H bond, that chain stops growing as P−H. The thiyl radical formed, RS·, adds to monomer and starts a new chain, so the number of radicals hardly changes; the effect on the polymerization rate stays small while each chain becomes shorter. This is why thiols are widely used industrially to control molecular weight. A thiol is not an initiator and does not increase the number of radicals. Trapping radicals to stop polymerization is the job of inhibitors such as hydroquinone, which are distinguished from chain-transfer agents by whether the radical formed starts polymerization again.

polymer-chem-011.question: A polystyrene has a weight-average molecular weight Mw of 1.04×10⁵ and a dispersity Mw/Mn of 2.0. Taking the formula weight of the repeat unit C8H8 as 104, which value is closest to the number-average degree of polymerization?
polymer-chem-011.explanation: First, the number-average molecular weight is Mn = Mw/(Mw/Mn) = 1.04×10⁵/2.0 = 5.2×10⁴. The number-average degree of polymerization is Mn divided by the formula weight of the repeat unit, 5.2×10⁴/104 = 5.0×10² (ignoring the mass of the end groups). 1.0×10³ divides Mw directly by the formula weight, giving the weight-average degree of polymerization, a different quantity from the number average. 2.5×10² divides by the dispersity a second time. The polystyrene repeat unit, −CH2−CH(C6H5)−, has the same composition as the styrene monomer, C8H8, which is characteristic of addition polymers. Thinking in terms of degree of polymerization lets you picture concretely how many monomers a chain contains from the molecular-weight figure.

polymer-chem-012.question: In radical copolymerization, what kind of copolymer tends to form from a pair of monomers with reactivity ratios r1 ≈ 0 and r2 ≈ 0 (for example, styrene and maleic anhydride)?
choices: A random copolymer in which the two monomers are arranged haphazardly in the feed ratio
A block copolymer in which long runs of the same monomer alternate with each other
An alternating copolymer in which the two monomers alternate one by one
polymer-chem-012.explanation: The reactivity ratio r1 = k11/k12 is the ratio of the rate constant for a radical ending in M1 adding another M1 to that for it adding the other monomer, M2. If r1 ≈ 0, an M1 end adds only M2, and if r2 ≈ 0, an M2 end adds only M1, so M1 and M2 alternate. Electron-rich styrene and electron-poor maleic anhydride are the classic example, and maleic anhydride hardly homopolymerizes at all. When r1·r2 = 1, the selectivity of addition is the same regardless of the chain end, so the monomers are arranged haphazardly, giving ideal (random) copolymerization. When r1 and r2 are both greater than 1, runs of the same monomer become likely, but block copolymers are usually made by living polymerization with sequential monomer addition.

polymer-chem-013.question: Monomers M1 and M2 were charged in equal molar amounts and radically copolymerized. The reactivity ratios are r1 = 2.0 and r2 = 0.5. Which value is closest to the mole fraction F1 of M1 in the copolymer formed early in the polymerization? Use the copolymer composition equation d[M1]/d[M2] = [M1](r1[M1] + [M2])/{[M2]([M1] + r2[M2])}.
polymer-chem-013.explanation: Because [M1] = [M2], the composition equation becomes d[M1]/d[M2] = (r1 + 1)/(1 + r2) = 3.0/1.5 = 2.0. The ratio of M1 to M2 in the copolymer is 2 : 1, so F1 = 2.0/(2.0 + 1) = 0.67. 0.50 assumes that the feed composition goes into the copolymer unchanged, which holds only when r1 = r2 = 1. 0.80 takes the ratio from the reactivity ratios alone, r1/(r1 + r2) = 2.0/2.5. This pair is an ideal copolymerization with r1·r2 = 1; because the more reactive M1 is incorporated more, the M1 remaining in the feed decreases as polymerization proceeds, and copolymer formed later contains more M2, a composition drift.

polymer-chem-014.question: A polymer solution was analyzed by gel permeation chromatography (GPC, size-exclusion chromatography). Which molecules elute first?
choices: The molecules with the smallest size in solution (hydrodynamic volume)
The molecules with the largest size in solution (hydrodynamic volume)
The highly polar molecules that adsorb most strongly on the stationary-phase surface
polymer-chem-014.explanation: A GPC column is packed with a porous gel, and components separate by how far they can enter the pores. Large molecules cannot enter the pores and pass only through the spaces between particles, so they elute first, while the smaller a molecule, the more pores it enters and the longer the path it travels, so it elutes later. Note that the elution order looks the reverse of ordinary chromatographic retention. The separation is assumed not to involve adsorption on or partition into the stationary phase; adsorption delays elution and leads to wrong molecular-weight estimates, so a solvent is chosen in which the polymer interacts little with the gel. Because separation is by size in solution rather than by molecular weight, care is also needed when comparing polymers of different shapes.

polymer-chem-015.question: Polystyrene standards measured by GPC eluted at 12.0 mL for molecular weight 1.0×10⁵ and at 18.0 mL for 1.0×10³. If log M is linear in elution volume, which value is closest to the polystyrene-equivalent molecular weight of a peak at an elution volume of 14.0 mL?
polymer-chem-015.explanation: The slope of the calibration line is (log 10³ − log 10⁵)/(18.0 − 12.0) = −2/6.0 ≈ −0.333 /mL. At 14.0 mL, log M = 5.00 − 0.333 × (14.0 − 12.0) = 4.33, so M = 10^4.33 ≈ 2.2×10⁴. 6.7×10⁴ interpolates the molecular weight itself linearly without taking logs, and 4.6×10³ interpolates 2.0 mL in the wrong direction from the low-molecular-weight standard (log M = 3.00 + 0.667). GPC values are relative, obtained by comparing size with standards, so they are written as "polystyrene equivalent", and for polymers of different shape they deviate from the true molecular weight. When absolute molecular weights are needed, a light-scattering detector is added.
